summary: This informational document describes the Media Server Control Markup Language, used with SIP to provide advanced conferencing and interactive voice response. It offers application-level rather than device-level control, for instance between a conference focus and mixer. It was replaced by RFC 5022.

eli5.summary: This is a language for telling a conference-call machine what to do, like asking it to play a message or mix voices, using simple instructions. It was later replaced by RFC 5022.

subtitle: XML language to control conferences and voice response over SIP.

tldr.problem: SIP alone cannot handle advanced conferencing features like multi-party mixing, participant control, or IVR operations. Applications need a way to tell a media server what to do with conference calls and voice interactions.
tldr.mechanism: MSCML is an XML markup language that clients send to media servers via SIP INVITE and INFO requests. It defines commands for conference setup, participant management, audio playback, DTMF collection, and recording.
tldr.outcome: This enables sophisticated telephony applications to control media servers at the application level. It was later superseded by RFC 5022, which unified related specifications.

facts.label: Main operations
facts.value: Conference control, IVR (play/collect/record), fax, event subscription

today: RFC 4722 is Informational and is no longer the current standard. It was superseded by RFC 5022 in 2008, which consolidated related specifications into a unified media server control framework.

sections.title: What MSCML Is and Does
sections.content:
MSCML (Media Server Control Markup Language) is a markup language used in conjunction with SIP to provide advanced conferencing and interactive voice response (IVR) functions. Instead of basic SIP mechanics that handle conference joins and leaves, MSCML lets applications send detailed commands to media servers that control mixing, participant configuration, audio playback, digit collection, and recording.

Prior to MSCML, there was no standard way to deliver these features over SIP. Applications needed device-level control protocols that were vendor-specific and complex. MSCML provides application-level control, meaning programmers work with conference and call concepts rather than raw media streams. It serves the interface between a conference focus (the controlling application) and a media mixer (the media server), as described in the IETF SIP Conferencing Framework.
sections.eli5: MSCML is instructions you give to a media server about what to do with a phone conference. Instead of just hanging up or joining, you can ask the server to mix voices, play sounds, or listen for button presses.

sections.title: Design Philosophy and XML Structure
sections.content:
MSCML follows a peer-to-peer programming model rather than master-slave. This means the media server can be used simultaneously by multiple applications, not locked to a single point of control. Standard SIP mechanisms handle media server location and load balancing. Clients identify themselves to the media server using SIP service indicators: "conf" for conferencing and "ivr" for voice response applications.

MSCML uses XML as a text-based description language for readability. It defines three element trees: <request> for commands sent by the client, <response> for replies from the server, and <notification> for events the server sends asynchronously. Each request or response body is wrapped in a <MediaServerControl> element. Payloads are sent inside SIP INVITE (for initial requests) or INFO (for mid-call requests) messages, allowing integration with standard SIP call setup and teardown.
sections.eli5: MSCML uses a simple text format (XML) so humans can read it. A client asks the server for something, the server does it, and sometimes the server sends back surprising news.

sections.title: Advanced Conferencing Capabilities
sections.content:
MSCML defines a star-controller model for conferences, where signaling and media flow through a central point. The application server acts as the conference focus, and the media server is the mixer. In this model, the first INVITE to the media server can include a <configure_conference> command that sets parameters like the number of expected participants. This creates a Conference Control Leg, a SIP dialog that controls the entire conference. As long as this leg exists, the conference persists, even if no participants are present.

Once a conference is created, clients can issue commands on the Conference Control Leg to play announcements to all participants, record the conference, request active talker reports, or configure personalized mixes where different participants hear different audio. On individual participant legs, clients can mute a participant, configure their audio settings, or send them to a waiting room. The media server also supports video conferencing through video switching: it sends the video of the loudest speaker to all other participants.
sections.eli5: A conference has one control button that the application holds. Using it, the app can play sounds to everyone, mute someone, or ask the server who is talking. Each person on the call has their own settings too.

sections.title: Interactive Voice Response (IVR) Operations
sections.content:
MSCML enables sophisticated IVR by allowing servers to play prompts, collect DTMF digits (key presses), and record audio. Prompts are specified using the <prompt> element, which can reference audio files (via HTTP or file URLs) or dynamic content from URLs. The prompt element supports many playback options: repeat count, delay between repetitions, gain (volume) adjustment, playback rate, offset into the file, and locale selection for spoken variables.

The <playcollect> request plays a prompt and waits for digit input. It can apply DTMF grammars to validate input, configure digit buffering and barge-in behavior (allowing the caller to interrupt), and set timers for input collection. The <playrecord> request combines playing a prompt with recording the caller's response. When a client sends a new IVR request while another is in progress, the server stops the first operation and reports what was collected so far. IVR commands on the Conference Control Leg affect the entire conference; commands on individual legs affect only that participant.
sections.eli5: MSCML can ask a caller a question by playing a voice message, wait for them to press buttons, listen to their voice, or all three. It is flexible about how the audio plays and what rules it enforces on the input.

sections.title: Content Management and Status Today
sections.content:
MSCML supports additional operations for managing stored content, sending and receiving faxes, and subscribing to call leg events like DTMF keypresses. The <managecontent> request allows clients to retrieve, delete, or modify content on the media server. The <faxplay> and <faxrecord> operations extend IVR to fax transmission and reception. Call leg event subscriptions let applications receive notifications of signal events (like ringing or busy) and keypress events as they occur during a call.

RFC 4722 is an Informational document describing a working framework with considerable implementation experience since 2001. However, it was obsoleted by RFC 5022, which consolidated and refined the specification. The protocol is no longer the current standard for media server control over SIP, though systems using it remain operational.
sections.eli5: MSCML can also manage sound files, handle fax, and let the app know when the caller presses a key. However, a newer version replaced it in 2008.
